newsitem.title: CHINA: China brokerages vie for convertible bond issues.
newsitem.headline: China brokerages vie for convertible bond issues.

text.p: China brokerage firms are scrambling to secure a share of a huge new market in corporate convertible bonds created this month by Beijing's securities authorities, analysts said on Friday.
Top non-listed state-run enterprises will be allowed to apply to issue the convertible bonds, up to a total value of four billion yuan, leading eventually to their public listing.
It is the first time convertible bonds will be issued in China on a large scale, and will push a whole new group of state firms in the direction of flotation.
"Securities firms are finding the competition very tough because everyone wants to break into this new area, even if there is no profit to be made initially," said a Shanghai brokerage analyst.
The prospect of this new market, so far viewed only as experimental by authorities, has also galvanised brokerages in the southern city of Shenzhen, home of China's second stock exchange.
"We have been busily contacting possible issuers but are facing increasing competition from other securities firms," a Shenzhen J&A Securities analyst said.
In the frenzy to grab a share of the market, brokerages may be overestimating the profits and neglecting to examine potential issuers for hidden problems, analysts said.
All the country's top 500 state enterprises are theoretically able to apply to issue the bonds, but in fact analysts say a large proportion of them would be ineligible.
The firms are required to have been in profit for three years in a row, which will be a major hurdle given the indebtedness of China's state sector.

Many of the firms are poorly managed with messy financial structures involving large amounts of unrecoverable debt, which would make them unattractive to even the most enthusiastic investor, analysts said.
"Candidates need to meet both profit and size requirements and need good management," said one analyst. "They need to be able to handle the requirements of the auditors."
But the brokerages want to sign up the good prospects as soon as possible.

"This is a new line of business," an analyst at China Guotai Securities in Beijing said. "We want to gain experience for when more such issues are allowed, assuming the experiment proves to be a success."
The bonds, if converted, will become shares in the issuing state firms and will be listed on the stock exchanges in either Shanghai or Shenzhen.
Under existing rules, the size of each convertible bond offer must be a minimum of 100 million yuan. The bonds must have a term of no less than three years and no more than five years.
China has previously only allowed a handful of convertible bond issues by some public firms, which tend to be more transparent and more used to meeting the requirements of regulators, analysts said.
But even with that handful there have been problems.
A 500-million-yuan convertible bond issue in 1992 by China Baoan Group Co Ltd, a large conglomerate listed in Shenzhen, proved to be a failure.
Only three percent of the bonds were converted into stock by maturity because the share markets were in a slump for most of the life of the issue, a Baoan spokeswoman said.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission, the country's top securities watchdog, will begin accepting convertible bond issue applications early next month, but the timing of the launch for the first issue is not yet known, analysts said.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
